source: Penn, Holyoak, Povinelli (2008) Darwin's mistake: explaining the discontinuity between human and nonhuman minds
finding: Core thesis. Human and nonhuman minds differ in a deep way: only humans approximate a physical symbol system, with higher-order, systematic, relational reasoning. The gap runs through nearly every cognitive domain and is deeper than language or culture alone explains.
numbers: Target article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences. No single experiment; a review of many paradigms. About 1,176 citations (OpenAlex).
quote: significant discontinuity in the degree to which human and nonhuman animals are able to approximate the higher-order, systematic, relational capabilities of a physical symbol system
limits: Only the abstract was read this session (Europe PMC); the full text was not reachable. Details of the argument come via later papers that cite it.
agent_relevance: The agent is a language model that can state relations in text. The named gap is a reason to build explicit relational steps (O7) into the scaffold rather than trust implicit similarity.

source: Penn, Holyoak, Povinelli (2008) Darwin's mistake: explaining the discontinuity between human and nonhuman minds (abstract: proposed mechanism)
finding: The authors propose a representational-level account of where animals match humans and where they differ. They suggest symbolic-connectionist models explain the mechanism of the gap.
numbers: Same abstract. No numbers.
limits: Abstract only. Competing view: continuity accounts (Thompson and Oden; Fagot; Cook and Wasserman) say the gap is one of degree.
agent_relevance: The gap is framed as role-filler binding, which a transformer does only by learned attention, not by design.

source: Fagot and Maugard (2013) Analogical reasoning in baboons (Papio papio): flexible reencoding of the source relation depending on the target relation
finding: Four baboons learned a two-dimensional relational matching-to-sample (RMTS) task in which the relevant dimension (colour or shape) was only revealed by the comparison pairs after the sample vanished. This forces re-encoding of the stored source relation.
numbers: Exp 1, Test Phase 1: 4 male Guinea baboons on touchscreens; six 120-trial blocks (60 colour, 60 shape). Mean 77% correct (range 74.9-80.8%). Training took 5-6 weeks with block size shrinking 120, 80, 40, 16, 8, 4, 2 trials; 80% correct needed in each block.
limits: Extensively trained animals, tiny N. The authors say the design rules out Penn et al.'s variability account; that is contested.
agent_relevance: Re-encoding a stored relation after seeing the target is like re-reading a problem after forming a hypothesis. It can be trained, but it is not free.

source: Fagot and Maugard (2013) Analogical reasoning in baboons (Papio papio): flexible reencoding of the source relation depending on the target relation (Exp 1 inconsistent trials and probes)
finding: Inconsistent trials (colour and shape signal different relations) were much harder than consistent ones. Cross-mapping probes were also tested.
numbers: Consistent vs inconsistent shape trials 96.3% vs 62.2%. Colour 94.3% vs 55.4%. Inconsistent trials still above chance (68.5% colour, 70.2% shape, all p<.0001). Test Phase 2: baseline 78.5% vs cross-mapping probes 76.9%.
limits: Per-animal variation. Interference from the irrelevant dimension is large, so perceptual cues compete with the relation.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant features that agree or disagree with the relation change accuracy a lot. Strip surface features before relational steps.

source: Fagot and Maugard (2013) Analogical reasoning in baboons (Papio papio): flexible reencoding of the source relation depending on the target relation (Exp 2 cross-dimensional matching)
finding: Baboons matched a relation shown by colour in the sample to the same relation shown by shape in the comparison. Three of four animals beat chance on the probes.
numbers: Exp 2: baseline 76.6% (range 74.7-81.6%), cross-dimensional probes 63.4% (range 54.4-76.2%). Three animals (CAUET, DAN, VIVIEN) above chance on probes, p<.01; the fourth was not. Block effect not significant, F(9,27)=.85, p>.05.
limits: Probe accuracy far below baseline and one animal failed. The claim rests on 3 animals.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain relation transfer exists but is fragile. Add explicit checks when the agent maps across domains.

source: Fagot and Maugard (2013) Analogical reasoning in baboons (Papio papio): flexible reencoding of the source relation depending on the target relation (historical review inside the paper)
finding: Timeline: Premack (1983) found language-trained chimp Sarah solved RMTS. Later apes without language training mostly failed (Oden et al. 1988, 1990; Flemming et al. 2007). Thompson, Oden and Boysen (1997) succeeded after token training. Baboons (Fagot et al. 2001) and pigeons (Cook and Wasserman 2007) solved it with arrays. Monkeys passed pair-RMTS after extensive training (Fagot and Parron 2010; Fagot and Thompson 2011; Truppa et al. 2011). Vonk (2003) reported gorillas and orangutans with limited training.
numbers: Dates and species as cited. No new numbers.
limits: Secondary account of other studies. Only Cook 2007 and Truppa 2011 were opened here.
agent_relevance: The claim that language is required has shrunk over 30 years. Symbols look like a scaffold, which supports a text scaffold for a model.

source: Cook and Wasserman (2007) Learning and transfer of relational matching-to-sample by pigeons
finding: Four pigeons learned to match 16-icon arrays by higher-order relation (both same, both different, or one of each) and transferred to icon sets with no shared items.
numbers: 4 pigeons; 4x4 grids of 16 icons from five non-overlapping sets of 20. Phase 1 symmetry test (reversed sample/test sets): 45.3% vs baseline 79.1%. Phase 2 novel sets: Set 3 60.8%, Set 4 59.2%. Retest transfer 70.1% vs baseline 75.7%. Phase 3 symmetry transfer 77.4% vs baseline 75.8%. Same-trial accuracy 74.3%, higher than different-trial.
limits: Transfer was imperfect and grew across phases (learning to transfer). Only 2 of 3 pigeons transferred in Phase 4. Arrays give variability cues, which Penn et al. say can solve the task without relations.
agent_relevance: A bird solves relational matching only after training and with entropy cues. A weak baseline for what an untrained system should do.

source: Truppa et al. (2011) Same/different concept learning by capuchin monkeys in matching-to-sample tasks
finding: Of five tufted capuchins, only one (Roberta) learned relational matching with 2-icon and 4-icon stimuli, after thousands of trials. First evidence in a New World monkey.
numbers: Exp 1 (small sets): mean 11,639 trials to criterion on the first set (Sandokan 4,839; Roberta 9,908; Robot 20,170). Exp 2: all five near chance after 100 96-trial sessions (means 49-55%). Roberta needed 77 sessions (7,392 trials) to flip a same-trial bias, then 228 sessions (21,888 trials) to reach about 70%. Novel-stimulus transfer: 4-icon 65.6%, 2-icon 67.7%, 16-icon 66.7%.
limits: Only 1 of 5 animals passed. Ceiling about 70%. Large sets with rising entropy did not help the group.
agent_relevance: Learning this relation takes 10^4 trials in a monkey. A language model does it in context with zero task training, which is a real difference.

source: Smith, Jackson, Church (2019) Breaking the perceptual-conceptual barrier: relational matching and working memory
finding: Humans in RMTS with the perceptual cue gradually faded had to find the abstract relational solution. A concurrent working-memory load made them fail to cross this barrier unless the load was dropped.
numbers: Georgia State undergraduates: control N=53 (matching .913 correct), concurrent-load N=51 (.865). Number task .938 vs .833. 43 of 53 controls (80%) dropped similarity level fast; the other 20% stalled in the 60s. Trial-block effect F(15,1530)=234.6, p<.001.
limits: Student sample. The barrier is probabilistic; some humans fail it without any load.
agent_relevance: Finding the relational construal needs working memory and explicit processing. A scaffold that makes the relation explicit in context may stand in for that load.

source: Smith, Jackson, Church (2019) Breaking the perceptual-conceptual barrier: relational matching and working memory (summary of animal failures)
finding: Review of failed monkey attempts: Smith et al. (2013) faded perceptual cues in rhesus macaques and RMTS performance collapsed. Flemming et al. (2011) used differential rewards and monkeys still failed. Fagot and Thompson (2011): 6 of 29 baboons met 80% after 15,000-30,000 trials.
numbers: 6 of 29 baboons passed, 15k-30k trials. Humans in the matched task: 99% correct overall.
limits: Account of earlier work by a partisan lab (working-memory story).
agent_relevance: Roughly one in five baboons and no macaques pass, versus nearly all humans.

source: Flemming et al. (2008) What meaning means for same and different: analogical reasoning in humans, chimpanzees and rhesus monkeys
finding: With meaningful stimuli humans acquired RMTS faster. Chimpanzees varied: meaning helped some and hurt others. Rhesus monkeys failed with or without meaningful stimuli.
numbers: Species: humans, chimpanzees, rhesus monkeys. Per-animal numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Author list and sample sizes not verified.
agent_relevance: Meaningful content changes relational performance. For LLMs, abstract symbols versus meaningful words may give different relational accuracy.

source: Hodgetts, Close, Hahn (2023) Similarity and structured representation in human and nonhuman apes
finding: Chimpanzees and gorillas show sensitivity to structural (relational) information in similarity judgments, mainly for colour-plus-shape stimuli, but are more featural for artificial shape stimuli.
numbers: Task 1: 5 chimps + 3 gorillas, 10 humans. Task 2: 4 chimps + 3 gorillas. Best model structural (RD): humans 98% variance (Task 1) and 90% (Task 2); apes 58% (Task 1); in Task 2 the apes' best was featural CS-FEAT at 98%. Species x task interaction F(1,15)=14.99, p=.002; Task 2 species difference p<.001 (BF10=594.6); Task 1 p=.45.
limits: Tiny N. Task 2 stimuli unfamiliar. Result depends on stimulus familiarity, a boundary condition on the gap.
agent_relevance: Relational competence depends on familiarity of material. Test the agent on familiar and unfamiliar relation material separately.

source: Hodgetts, Close, Hahn (2023) Similarity and structured representation in human and nonhuman apes (per-subject fits)
finding: Per-subject best-fit model was structural for 8/10 humans in Task 1 and 10/10 in Task 2. For apes it moved from 8/8 structural (Task 1) to 5/7 featural (Task 2).
numbers: Human structurality did not differ between tasks (p=.62, BF10=.35). Apes more featural in Task 2 (p=.005, BF10=10.82).
limits: The task contrast is the whole story. No evidence of a general ape inability.
agent_relevance: The gap is context dependent, not a switch.

source: Martin-Ordas (2023) Relational reasoning in wild bumblebees revisited: the role of distance
finding: Wild bumblebees spontaneously matched objects rather than relations, but only when the objects were far apart. Near objects gave no clear preference. This questions whether relational focus is the animal pattern.
numbers: Exp 1: condition effect z=-3.20, P=0.001. Distant: object matching above chance (W=102, P=0.002) and preferred over spatial (W=3, P=0.002). Near: no preference (W=31, P=0.891). Controls above chance (Distant W=45, P=.005; Near W=48, P=.036). 33% of bees used a relational strategy, 40% an object strategy. Exp 2 (colour, 29 bees): no condition effect (z=-0.824, P=0.410). Exp 3 (shape): 30 bees.
limits: Spatial-search paradigm, not RMTS. Small samples of wild-caught bees.
agent_relevance: Framing can flip relation-versus-surface strategy. State which one the agent should use.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on several analogy tasks. Full numbers are in evidence_b b01.
numbers: Cross-reference: digit matrices OR 1.88 (generative) and 6.27 (multiple choice); letter strings OR 1.76.
limits: Cross-reference; not re-read for this file.
agent_relevance: At 2022-23 scale, LLMs reach human level on text analogies with no task training. The question moves from capacity to robustness.

source: Webb, Frankland, Altabaa et al. (2024) The relational bottleneck as an inductive bias for efficient abstraction
finding: Review of models that force a network to see relations among inputs rather than input attributes. Offers a reconciliation of connectionist and symbolic accounts and a candidate mechanism for the human advantage Penn et al. described.
numbers: Review paper. States that children learn relational tasks from fewer than about 20 examples, versus very large training sets for standard nets.
limits: Review; the human sample-efficiency figure is cited, not new data. Cites Penn et al. 2008.
agent_relevance: Design principle: separate relation from content. A scaffold can ask the model to restate the problem as roles and relations before solving (O7).

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory
finding: A network with external memory that binds keys to values learns same/different and relational match-to-sample rules from about 10^4 problems and generalises to new symbols, where standard nets fail.
numbers: Same/different test accuracy (10 nets), regime m=95 (95 of 100 image classes held out in training): ESBN+TCN 100.0, Transformer 73.7, LSTM 61.8, Relation Network 50.5. At m=98: ESBN+TCN 100.0, Transformer+TCN 72.3, Transformer 56.1. RMTS m=95: ESBN+TCN 95.0, Transformer 49.9, Relation Network 50.0. ESBN without TCN was near 50% on same/different.
limits: Toy image tasks. Needs the temporal context normalisation trick.
agent_relevance: A computational model of the relations-between-relations gap: plain networks fail out of distribution on same/different like untrained animals.

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (distribution-of-three)
finding: On the Raven-like distribution-of-three task, ESBN stays near perfect where other nets fall to chance at the hardest split.
numbers: m=95: ESBN+TCN 99.7, ESBN 62.0, Transformer+TCN 32.1, Transformer 28.0, Relation Network 25.2. Chance is 25% (four options).
limits: Averages over 10 nets. Synthetic images.
agent_relevance: Standard sequence models sit at chance on novel content; relational structure is not picked up by default.

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (task design as OOD ladder)
finding: Graded held-out regimes (m = 0, 50, 85, 95, 98) provide a ladder of increasing out-of-distribution difficulty for same/different, RMTS, distribution-of-three and identity rules.
numbers: Training sets about 10^4 problems; the paper cites Fagot et al. (2001) on baboons as motivation.
limits: Synthetic images; animals only cited, not tested.
agent_relevance: A graded OOD ladder is a template for testing relational transfer in our agent.

source: Altabaa, Webb, Cohen, Lafferty (2024) Abstractors and relational cross-attention
finding: A Transformer extension (Abstractor) with relational cross-attention separates relations from object features and gives large sample-efficiency gains on relational sequence tasks and maths tasks.
numbers: SET task split: 50% train, 15% validation, 35% test. Sorting learning curves run from 100 to 3,000 samples in steps of 100. Exact gains were shown only in figures and not extracted.
limits: Figures only. Small synthetic tasks plus a maths dataset.
agent_relevance: Standard transformers need many examples for pure relational tasks. Explicit relation representation in the prompt is the cheap analogue.

source: Thompson and Oden (2000) The paleological monkey and the analogical ape
finding: Proposed that only apes, not monkeys or nonprimates, can judge relations between relations. Stated second-hand in Cook and Wasserman (2007).
numbers: No numbers; second-hand.
limits: Page blocked. Later results (baboons, capuchin Roberta, pigeons) contradict the strict species cut.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap framed as graded by species, like graded model scale.

source: Premack (1983) The codes of man and beasts
finding: Reported that the language-trained chimpanzee Sarah matched relations between relations. Premack concluded symbol training is needed for second-order relations.
numbers: Second-hand via Fagot and Maugard (2013).
limits: Not opened. Oden, Thompson and Premack (1988, 1990) found untrained apes failed.
agent_relevance: Symbols as scaffold for relational thought is the animal version of a text scaffold for a model.

source: Thompson, Oden, Boysen (1997) Language-naive chimpanzees judge relations between relations
finding: Chimpanzees trained with arbitrary tokens for same and different matched relations between relations without language training.
numbers: Second-hand via Fagot and Maugard (2013), which calls it a notable exception.
limits: Not opened; URL is a search link, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Token labels for relations resemble giving the agent named relation labels.

source: Fagot, Wasserman, Young (2001) Discriminating the relation between relations: the role of entropy in abstract conceptualization by baboons and humans
finding: Baboons learned same/different over arrays and showed entropy effects similar to humans.
numbers: Second-hand via the reference list of Webb et al. (2021) and Fagot and Maugard (2013).
limits: Not opened; URL is a search link. Array entropy can supply a perceptual cue, the Penn et al. objection.
agent_relevance: Array tasks may be solved by variability, not relations. Check that LLM tests have no such loophole.

source: Penn et al. (2008) variability objection as restated by Fagot and Maugard (2013)
finding: Penn et al. argued primate RMTS successes could come from estimates of perceptual variability in source and target, not relations per se.
numbers: Fagot and Maugard say their cross-mapping and re-encoding design rules this out.
limits: Fagot and Maugard are on the continuity side; whether it is fully ruled out is contested.
agent_relevance: The variability shortcut is the animal version of passing a test via surface statistics. Use probes that break the shortcut.

source: Smith, Jackson, Church (2019) Breaking the perceptual-conceptual barrier: relational matching and working memory (implication)
finding: The authors argue the perceptual-conceptual barrier is a qualitative reconstrual of the task, depending on explicit working-memory processes, and that animals' limits here matter for the gap debate.
numbers: 43 of 53 controls moved quickly; 20% hit a wall at similarity level in the 60s.
limits: Interpretation is the authors', not shown directly for animals.
agent_relevance: Suggests a two-stage scaffold: notice the relation, then apply it. Noticing is the costly step.
